llm.answer: This is most likely an FAA NPRM for Airbus Canada Limited Partnership (formerly Bombardier) A220-100 and A220-300 airplanes, which carry the type designations BD-500-1A10 and BD-500-1A11. It would propose an AD addressing low clearance between the hydraulic motor pump (HMP) wiring harness and adjacent structure, which could cause chafing, arcing and a possible fire or loss of hydraulic function. The proposed fix would be an inspection of the clearance, followed by repositioning or replacing the harness or adding protection. I am not certain of the docket number cited above, so please verify it against the Federal Register.

I believe this is the FAA NPRM for Airbus SAS Model A330-841 and A330-941 airplanes. It would require inspecting and replacing engine fire extinguisher bottles that have cracks at the discharge outlet, based on a related EASA AD. I am not certain of the docket number cited (FAA-2023-2002) and could not confirm it from memory, so please check it against the Federal Register.

I believe this is a Boeing Model 787 series (787-8, -9, -10) NPRM under 14 CFR Part 39. It would address missing sealing tape at the cargo compartment liner joints, which could compromise the cargo fire-protection and containment function. I cannot recall the FR document number or docket number with confidence, so I won't cite one. Check the Federal Register for a recent 'Airworthiness Directives; The Boeing Company Airplanes' NPRM that covers 787 cargo liner joint sealing tape.

I could not recall the FR document number or docket number for this NPRM, and I would rather not invent one. My best recollection is that it is a Boeing 787-8/-9/-10 NPRM covering the left engine fan cowl. The concern is that the cowl may lack adequate protection against debris from an uncontained failure of the opposite (cross-engine) engine. From memory, the proposed action is a one-time inspection (a general visual or detailed check) to confirm that the fan cowl has the required protective configuration, such as the correct part number or shielding. If it does not, the NPRM would require corrective action, either modification or replacement, per the Boeing service information. Please verify the specifics against the Federal Register notice itself.

I am working from memory and could not confirm this. The best match I can offer is a Boeing 757 NPRM (Part 39, The Boeing Company Airplanes) covering fatigue cracking in the lower lobe fuselage frames at existing reinforcing repairs. It would require repetitive inspections and repair or modification per a Boeing service bulletin. I could not recall the exact FR document number, so the docket number cited is a low-confidence guess.

I could not recall the specific NPRM that supersedes AD 2023-12-16 for Rolls-Royce Trent 1000 engines, so I cannot give its document or docket number. My best recollection is that the proposal revises the earlier AD's inspection and life-limit requirements after Rolls-Royce introduced a new engine hardware modification and updated the Time Limits Manual. This part is low confidence and should be checked against the Federal Register.

I could not confirm this from memory. AD 2009-04-13 covers Rolls-Royce Deutschland BR700-715 series turbofan engines. My best recollection is that the superseding NPRM is a Rolls-Royce Deutschland BR700-715 proposal filed under Docket No. FAA-2013-0457. I cannot give its FR document number with confidence, so treat the docket number as a guess to verify.

Most likely not. AD 2025-13-11 and the proposed AD that would supersede it address spoiler electrical units (spoiler control/actuation electronics) on Dassault Falcon 7X airplanes only. A Falcon 2000 is a different type certificate and model, so it is not in the applicability section. I am working from memory and cannot give a Federal Register or docket number for the NPRM. Check the applicability paragraph of the NPRM and confirm your airplane's type certificate and model designation. Falcon 2000 variants (2000, 2000EX, 2000DX, 2000LX, 2000S, 2000LXS) are not Falcon 7X models.

I have no access to the text of the proposed AD in docket FAA-2026-1338 and cannot identify its FR document number, so I cannot confirm its applicability from my own knowledge. The A330-243 is an A330-200 series model, and Airbus A330 NPRMs usually list it among the affected models. However, applicability normally depends on the manufacturer serial number and on whether a production or service-bulletin modification is already embodied. An aircraft with a certificate of airworthiness issued 2026-03-01 is a very recent build, so it may be excluded if it left the factory with the modification. Check the NPRM's applicability paragraph and the referenced EASA AD or Airbus service information against your aircraft's MSN and modification status.

I don't have the contents of docket FAA-2026-1338, so I can't confirm its applicability or give a Federal Register document number for the latest NPRM. The A330-243 is an A330-200 series model with Rolls-Royce Trent 700 engines. It is included in many Airbus A330 ADs that list the A330-200 series, and it is often named explicitly, but not always. To decide, open the docket and read the Applicability paragraph, which lists the models, and the referenced Airbus service information. Then check your aircraft's manufacturer serial number, any installed modifications or service bulletins, and, for engine or component ADs, the part numbers. The AD applies only if your A330-243 matches the listed models and those conditions.

Likely yes. I could not check the proposed rule text, so this comes from memory and is not verified. Proposed ADs on Airbus Helicopters main rotor servo-control nut torque normally cover the AS350 family, which includes the AS350B3. They usually apply to helicopters with the affected servo-control installed, whatever the serial number. Check the applicability paragraph and the servo-control part numbers in FAA-2026-11814, and confirm that no listed modification or servo-control replacement already exempts your aircraft. If your servo-controls are not the listed part numbers, the AD would not apply to you.

This is a best guess from memory, not a verified reading of the NPRM. Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 747-28A2373 RB is an ATA 28 (fuel system) bulletin, and the Boeing 747-400 is, as far as I recall, among the models it covers. On that basis the proposed AD likely applies to your 747-400. I could not recall the FR document number or docket number, so I have not cited one. Applicability is normally limited to the airplane groups and line numbers listed in the bulletin's effectivity table, so please check your airplane's serial number against the NPRM's applicability paragraph and the bulletin's effectivity before relying on this.

I can't confirm from memory what FAA-2025-2277 covers or its exact applicability, and I don't know its Federal Register document number. BD-700-2A12 is the Bombardier Global 7500 type certificate model. The proposed AD applies only if that model, and the specific serial numbers listed in its applicability paragraph, are named. Check the NPRM's applicability section and the service information it cites against your aircraft's serial number. Also check whether any modification or service bulletin it references has already been embodied on your aircraft.

I can't confirm applicability. I have no documents available and can't reliably recall a specific CF34-8C5 NPRM that lists EEC/FADEC P/N 4120T00P30, so I won't invent a document or docket number. A CF34-8C5 engine is generally within the type-design scope of CF34-8C-series ADs, but whether this proposed AD applies depends on its applicability paragraph and any software or part-number criteria. Check whether P/N 4120T00P30 (or its installed software version) is listed in the NPRM's applicability section or in the referenced GE service bulletin. If it is listed, the AD applies. If it isn't, it likely doesn't apply, unless the AD covers all CF34-8C5 engines regardless of EEC part number.

I can't confirm applicability. I have no source text for the proposed AD, and I can't reliably recall a specific NPRM or document number that lists EEC/FADEC part number 4120T00P99 for the CF34-8C5. Your engine model is CF34-8C5, so it is likely within the AD's model applicability. However, proposed ADs that target the EEC usually apply only to specific EEC part numbers or software versions. Check the applicability paragraph and the service information (GE service bulletin) cited in the NPRM to see whether 4120T00P99 is listed. Also confirm the installed EEC software version. If the part number is not listed, the AD would not apply unless the unit is modified to an affected configuration. Check the Federal Register notice for the exact document and docket numbers.

I can't confirm applicability. I have no document in front of me and can't identify the specific NPRM or cite a reliable FR or docket number without guessing. The CF34-8C5 is a GE engine model, so an AD aimed at CF34-8C series engines could cover it. Applicability for FADEC/EEC-related ADs usually depends on the EEC part number or software version installed, so a CF34-8C5 model match alone doesn't settle it. Check the Applicability paragraph of the NPRM for the listed engine models and the EEC part number or software version. Then compare those with your engine's data plate and EEC records, or ask GE or the FAA engine certification office.

I can't confirm from memory that this proposed AD was revised. I don't know of a supplemental NPRM or reopened comment period for docket FAA-2025-2277 (Bombardier BD-700-2A12). I also can't give a Federal Register document number for one. My best guess is that only the original NPRM was published, with no revision, but this is unverified. Check the docket on regulations.gov for any SNPRM.

An NPRM is a proposed rule, so it is not the final version by definition. The final version would be a separate final rule AD, which comes after the comment period. I have no reliable knowledge of a supplemental NPRM (SNPRM), a revised NPRM, or a final rule in docket FAA-2025-5394, and I cannot give a Federal Register document number for one. Treat it as the original NPRM unless the docket on regulations.gov shows a later SNPRM or final rule. Check that docket to confirm.

I can't confirm the current status from memory, and I don't recall the Federal Register document number for this NPRM. An NPRM stays pending until the FAA publishes a final rule (an airworthiness directive) or withdraws the proposal. The comment period has probably closed, but the proposal is likely still pending unless a final rule has appeared. To confirm, check docket FAA-2025-0204 on regulations.gov and search the Federal Register for a final rule or withdrawal notice on the Boeing 787 tuning control panel software.

I can't confirm this from memory. I don't reliably know the FR document or docket number for a Dassault Falcon 7X spoiler electrical unit AD, so I won't invent one. An NPRM is only a proposal and has no force. A final AD takes effect on the effective date stated in its Federal Register publication, usually about 30 to 35 days after publication. If a final rule has been published and that date has passed, the AD is in force. Check the final rule's effective date in the Federal Register or the FAA Dynamic Regulatory System.

I can't confirm from memory whether line/serial number 41234 is in the effectivity listing of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-55A1104 RB. Effectivity is set by the bulletin's own table of airplane line numbers, and I can't reliably recall that table. I also can't tie the bulletin to a specific FAA NPRM or AD number without guessing, so I am not citing one. A 737-800 can be listed, but that depends on the line number and on whether the bulletin's actions have already been done. To check, look at the effectivity section of the bulletin (available through MyBoeingFleet) and the applicability paragraph of the related AD or NPRM. Also compare the airplane's manufacturer serial number and line number with the bulletin's listed groups. Note that 41234 would need to match Boeing's MSN format for the 737NG.

I don't know of any FAA airworthiness directive (final rule or NPRM) for the Antonov An-124, and I won't invent a document number. The An-124 has no FAA type certificate. Its state of design is Ukraine, and the Ukrainian authority (State Aviation Administration of Ukraine, with Antonov) issues its continued-airworthiness mandates. FAA ADs under 14 CFR Part 39 are normally written for products with a US type certificate. To be sure, search the FAA Dynamic Regulatory System (DRS) and the Federal Register for 'Antonov' and check your aircraft's registry authority's airworthiness requirements. Without your registration country and serial number, I can't say definitively whether any mandatory airworthiness action applies to your aircraft.
